notes.key_messages: • Candidates need to be able to provide clear and precise definitions of business terms. • Many candidates missed application marks. Candidates should be encouraged to use information from the stem to help answer part (c) and part (d) questions as this provides the basis for application. • Candidates should use a different point of application for each point made. The same analysis point should not be used for both points within the same question. • Evaluation is more than a decision, or a summary of earlier points made. Evaluation requires candidates to make a supported judgement which should follow on from points raised in the answer. It should clearly answer the question set. An example of an answer which includes evaluation can be found in the mark scheme for each part (e) question.
notes.general_comments: Overall, many candidates demonstrated good knowledge of concepts but found application, analysis and evaluation marks more challenging to obtain. This paper included some topics which candidates found challenging. It is important to remember that any area of the syllabus can be assessed. Part (a) and (b) of each question were generally well attempted. However, many candidates lacked the necessary precision in definitions or range of knowledge to access all the marks available. For most part (c) (excluding 3c which only assesses knowledge) and all part (d) questions, it is important candidates use the information from the stem to link their answers to the context. This helps ensure that any point raised is appropriate to the business. Candidates should use a different point of application for each point made. It is important to understand which skills are being assessed in each question. Many candidates continue to include analysis in part (c) questions and application in part (e) questions. However , the questions do not assess these skills so marks cannot be awarded. Most part (c) questions assess knowledge and application whilst part (e) assesses knowledge, analysis and evaluation. Candidates need to develop their evaluative skills. Of those who did attempt an evaluative comment, most were unable to provide reasoned statements to back up the decision made. One approach is to make a choice, provide a reason for this decision and then explain why it is better than the alternative option or viewpoint discussed.
notes.1a: This question was answered well by most candidates. A common mistake was to identify examples of primary sector activities. Others confused the term with the secondary sector.
notes.1b: For this question, where candidates who knew the formula to calculate current liabilities gained full marks. A common mistake was to include non-current liabilities in the total. Some answers were incorrect but were still able to gain one mark as they had included the correct working as part of their response.
notes.1c: Most responses evidenced good knowledge and stronger responses answers linked answers to the context to access the application marks. A common mistake was to identify external sources of finance. Instead of application, some responses described how the source worked. Others repeated the same application for both answers which can only be awarded once.
notes.1d: This was a challenging question for most candidates. Better responses recognised that a high level of debt could make it difficult for a business to gain more loans or lead to cashflow problems. However most struggled to develop these points. Application was rarely included which meant a missed opportunity to gain two additional marks. For example, responses could have included the bank loan of $200 000 or that this was a fishing business. A common mistake was to identify reasons why a business might have a high level of debt or offer solutions. There was a common misconception to assume profit is used to pay interest.
notes.1e: Many responses to this question demonstrated a good knowledge of methods. Many answers focused on using renewable energy and reducing the number of materials being extracted. Many responses attempted to link points to the context, however, this is a generic question and there are no marks for application. Most responses struggled to develop points. Many made vague comments about reducing pollution which applies to all methods, rather than explaining how the chosen methods could help achieve this. For example, extracting fewer resources would leave more for future generations. Some responses did make a decision, but invariably this was not supported by points made which was necessary for evaluation to be considered.
notes.2a: Most candidates recognised that a limited company had limited liability or could sell shares. Stronger responses were able to provide a precise definition. A common mistake was to define other terms such as a private limited company, public limited company, or private sector business. Others made vague statements about ‘not losing assets’ which could not be awarded.
notes.2b: This question was answered well by most candidates. The best responses included having a target and motivating employees. A common mistake was to repeat a similar point for both answers which can only be awarded once.
notes.2c: Most responses included good knowledge for this question. A common mistake was to repeat the same point of application for each answer. For example, instead of using shoes each time, responses could have mentioned the business made 18 000 pairs each week.
notes.2d: Most candidates were able to gain knowledge marks for recognising employees might want higher wages and suppliers may want to charge higher prices. However most struggled to analyse why these stakeholder objectives might create a conflict with GBR’s own objective. Many responses identified lower profit without explaining why this may happen. For example, higher wages could result in higher costs, and it is the higher costs which could lower profit. Many candidates attempted to apply their answers by recognising that the business made shoes.
notes.2e: This was a challenging question and poorly answered by most candidates. Those who gained knowledge marks understood that the size of the market could help determine the level of demand, and if high demand was expected then the business needed a method of production which could help meet this demand, otherwise it risked losing potential sales. Another way to access the knowledge marks was to identify other factors such as availability of suitable employees or initial cost. Better responses then went beyond this to compare the importance of each factor and attempted to use this information as the basis for evaluation. However, most responses struggled to make the link between size of the market, demand and the most suitable method. There were many vague statements about issues such as speed and type of market. Other incorrect answers simply described various methods of production.
notes.3a: This question was answered well. A common mistake was to repeat similar points, using different words. For example, earning money and pay for basic needs are alternative ways of expressing the same idea, and will only be awarded once.
notes.3b: Most responses either identified a trade union was a group formed of workers or it was an organisation that existed to protect rights. Stronger responses were able to provide a precise definition. A common mistake was to confuse the term with a pressure group.
notes.3c: Most candidates gained at least one knowledge mark for identifying growth. The strongest answers gained full marks for identifying all four stages of the business cycle. A common mistake was to confuse the term with product life cycle. Others identified the factors of production.
notes.3d: This question produced a range of responses. Stronger responses explained how induction training allowed new employees to become familiar with the workplace leading to fewer mistakes. Application marks were often awarded for recognising this was a hotel and had 20 employees. Most responses struggled to explain possible limitations. Some responses recognised it could be time consuming or increase cost but were not able to develop this into analysis. A common mistake was to confuse the method with on-the-job or off-the-job training. Others discussed general reasons why training was necessary.
notes.3e: This question was answered well by most candidates. Good knowledge of the interview stage was evident. Stronger responses were able to develop points to demonstrate why the stage was important. Common mistakes included identifying documents or describing activities rather than identifying specific stages in the recruitment process. Some responses identified additional points of knowledge or defined the terms which the question did not require and were unable to gain analysis marks. Most responses discussed points in the context of a hotel, which was unnecessary, and carried no marks.
notes.4a: Most answers lacked the necessary precision needed to gain both marks for this question. Some responses understood niche market represented a smaller segment of a market but were unable to provide a full definition. There were vague statements about the size of the market or assumptions made about the product such as it must be high-quality or have a high price. Others confused niche market with market segmentation.
notes.4b: This question was poorly answered by most candidates. Stronger responses identified points such as ‘avoid misleading advertising’ however, responses did not develop to identify a second impact. A common mistake was to discuss other areas of legal control concerning the environment or employment. Some responses confused legal controls with tariffs and quotas. Others repeated similar points for both impacts which can only be awarded once.
notes.4c: This question was answered well by most candidates who understood a good brand image could help increase customers or provide opportunities to charge higher prices. There was good application for this question as responses recognised this was a new business or that it made furniture. A common mistake was to forget to use different points of application to link each answer to the context, which meant responses could not be awarded the second application mark.
notes.4d: Most responses identified at least one reason, for example, increased competition. Weaker responses did not develop points to access analysis marks. Instead of development some responses repeated the knowledge or simply stated it would be a threat. There were also many vague statements about not ‘being seen’ without identifying why. For example, customers may have limited access to the internet. Application was often awarded for references to handmade furniture or niche market.
notes.4e: There were many good responses to this question. Stronger responses were able to explain why factors such as access to customers and cost of rent needed to be considered. For example, being close to customers could increase revenue. Weaker responses listed additional factors or repeated the knowledge point instead of offering any effective development. Any evaluation tended to be a decision, however, this usually lacked a supporting reason. BUSINESS STUDIES
